paras: The threatened lynching of William Russell took place near Frankfort, Kentucky, in November 1881, after Russell, a Black man, was jailed on a charge of assaulting a white woman, Mrs. Hutchinson. Threats of lynching were made on the night of his arrest, and they reportedly grew when Mrs. Hutchinson died of her injuries. No lynching was reported; the last account had Black men guarding the jail to protect him.

According to a Frankfort special to the Louisville Courier-Journal, Russell went to Mrs. Hutchinson's home near the Kentucky Military Institute on the evening of Wednesday, November 9, and assaulted her "with intent to commit rape." The dispatch said he knocked her down with a shovel, broke her arm and shot her in the shoulder, then ran. He was captured, brought to the city and lodged in jail.

That night, the dispatch reported, "great excitement prevails in the neighborhood, and threats of lynching are freely indulged in." A shorter version printed in Salt Lake City said Russell was "likely to be lynched to-night" for an assault "on a white woman for a fiendish purpose." Neither report identified who made the threats or gave a number.

A special to the Cincinnati Commercial, sent from Frankfort and dated from Cincinnati on November 12, reported that Mrs. Hutchinson, "an elderly woman," had died of her injuries. It said the prisoner had been threatened with lynching and that the probability of a lynching was "increased by the death of his victim." The same report stated that "Colored men are guarding the jail to protect the prisoner." No later report of an attack on the jail, an inquest into Mrs. Hutchinson's death, or a trial of Russell appears in the coverage.

The case was known to distant readers through two separate specials. The Courier-Journal dispatch ran on November 10 in the Rock Island Argus, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Chicago Daily Tribune, and over the following week in Salt Lake City, Dallas, Las Vegas and Jackson, Mississippi. Its headlines stressed race: "A Negro's Crime" in St. Paul, "A Lady Assaulted by a Negro" in Chicago, and "A Black Man Attempts a Black Deed" in Las Vegas. These papers stated the assault as fact and reported the lynching threats without comment.

The Commercial special, headed "Assaulted by a Negro," appeared in the Alexandria Gazette on November 12 and in the Daily Gazette on November 14, the latter with a "Frankford" dateline. It called Russell "a negro boy" rather than a man and was the only version to mention the Black guard at the jail.

The two specials disagree on Russell's first name: the Courier-Journal called him William and the Commercial called him Adam. The Courier-Journal dispatch, sent the night of the assault, reported Mrs. Hutchinson injured, while the later Commercial special reported her death, dated "yesterday" in one printing and "to-day" in the other.

Threats of lynching were reported in the neighborhood and Russell was said to be 'likely to be lynched to-night' (A2, A5), but the latest report has him in jail under a guard of colored men and no killing is reported (A4, A8).

Two separate specials, the Courier-Journal's (A1, A2, A5) and the Commercial's (A4, A8), agree that a Black man named Russell was jailed for assaulting Mrs. Hutchinson and was threatened with lynching.

accounts.label: Courier-Journal Frankfort special
accounts.gist: On the evening of Nov. 9 Russell assaulted Mrs. Hutchinson with intent to rape, struck her with a shovel, broke her arm and shot her; he ran, was captured and jailed, and that night threats of lynching were 'freely indulged in.'

accounts.label: Commercial (Cincinnati) special
accounts.gist: Mrs. Hutchinson, an elderly woman, died of injuries from the Wednesday assault by 'a negro boy named Adam Russell'; he had been threatened with lynching, the danger had grown with her death, and colored men were guarding the jail.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Courier-Journal dispatch under racial headlines such as 'A Negro's Crime' and 'A Black Man Attempts a Black Deed', treating the assault charge as fact.
The Commercial special, headed 'Assaulted by a Negro.', reported the lynching threat and the Black guard at the jail without comment.

conflicts.note: The two specials give different first names; the Courier-Journal version ran far more widely.

versions.value: Injured (arm broken, shot in the shoulder); no death reported

conflicts.note: The Courier-Journal dispatch was sent the night of the assault; the Commercial special came two or three days later. The 'yesterday'/'to-day' difference is the same special reprinted with altered tense.
A8 reprints the same Commercial special that A4 datelines Frankfort; 'Frankford' appears to be a misprint.
